sentences.text: And here is our home: Earth, the only place in the universe we know to harbor life. 71 percent of its surface is covered with liquid water; that is why it looks blue from space.
Let's move to the night side: city lights are the signature of a living planet, visible from space.
Its strong magnetic field protects us from the solar wind, and the ozone layer filters out ultraviolet rays.
This photograph, the Blue Marble, taken in 1972 by the crew of Apollo 17, became one of the most reproduced images in history.
The Moon's gravity keeps Earth's axial tilt steady, so the seasons stay regular; now let's pull back and watch its month-long trip.
Jupiter, king of the planets: its mass is two and a half times the total of all the other planets.
When we place a true-scale Earth beside it, the difference is striking: 1,300 Earths fit inside it.
It has no surface; the colored bands you see are giant cloud belts in an atmosphere of hydrogen and helium.
The Great Red Spot is a storm larger than Earth that has lasted at least 350 years.
This giant's day lasts only 10 hours; right now you are watching one Jupiter day sped up.
More than 95 known moons orbit it; Galileo discovered four of them in 1610 with his small telescope.
The Red Planet, Mars, takes its color from the rusted iron on its surface.
Its diameter is about half of Earth's; but its land area is almost equal to all of Earth's land, because it has no ocean.
It is home to the largest volcano in the Solar System: Olympus Mons, 22 kilometers high, is two and a half times Everest.
The Valles Marineris canyon, 4,000 kilometers long, is long enough to stretch clear across the American continent.
Billions of years ago there were rivers and lakes on its surface; today robots such as Curiosity and Perseverance are searching for traces of that water.
Its day is very similar to ours, 24 hours and 37 minutes; its year lasts 687 days.
Our first stop is Mercury: the smallest planet, and the closest to the Sun.
One trip around the Sun takes only 88 days; right now you are watching that trip sped up.
By contrast, it spins very slowly on its axis: one Mercury day lasts two Mercury years.
Its atmosphere is so thin it barely exists; that is why the dayside rises to 430 degrees while the nightside drops to minus 180 degrees.
The Caloris Basin in the northern hemisphere is a giant impact scar 1,500 kilometers wide; the collision that formed it raised hills even on the exact opposite side of the planet.
Right now BepiColombo, the joint spacecraft of Europe and Japan, is on its way to enter orbit around Mercury.
The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite, and the only other celestial body humans have set foot on.
Look how small it is beside Earth: its diameter is only about a quarter of Earth's.
In 1969 Apollo 11 landed in the Sea of Tranquility; Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the surface for two and a half hours.
By 1972 a total of 12 astronauts had walked on the Moon and brought back 382 kilograms of rock.
The bright-rayed Tycho Crater in the south is the mark of a collision 108 million years ago; its rays stretch for thousands of kilometers.
The Moon always shows us the same face, because its rotation is locked to its orbit; every year it moves about 4 centimeters farther away from us.
Neptune, the farthest planet from the Sun; it was discovered not with a telescope, but on paper.
Mathematicians studying the deviations in Uranus's orbit calculated its position, and in 1846 it was found right there.
One trip around the Sun takes 165 years; since its discovery it has completed only one trip.
Its winds exceed 2,100 kilometers per hour; these are the fastest winds in the Solar System.
When Voyager 2 flew past in 1989, it saw a storm the size of Earth: the Great Dark Spot.
Its large moon Triton orbits backwards; it is probably a captured Kuiper Belt object, and one day it will break apart and turn into a ring.
Our last stop is Pluto; it was discovered in 1930 and was considered the ninth planet until 2006.
In fact it is even smaller than our Moon: when we place them side by side, this is clearly visible.
Until New Horizons flew past in 2015, it was nothing more than a blurry dot.
The spacecraft found a giant heart shape on the surface, nitrogen glaciers and mountains of water ice; the surface temperature is minus 230 degrees.
Its moon Charon is so large that the two of them orbit together around a shared center of mass that lies in the space between them.
Our Solar System tour ends here; have a good journey.
Saturn is, without a doubt, the most elegant planet in the Solar System.
Its rings are made mostly of water ice, and they reach a width of 280,000 kilometers.
But when we look at them exactly edge-on, they almost disappear: in most places they are only about 10 meters thick.
The planet itself is so light that if you placed it in a large enough ocean, it would float.
At the north pole spins a mysterious hexagonal storm, each side as large as Earth.
The Cassini spacecraft studied this system for 13 years and, in 2017, completed its mission by diving into the planet's atmosphere.
Welcome to the Solar System tour; our journey begins at the center of everything, the Sun.
This star, four and a half billion years old, alone holds 99. 8 percent of the system's total mass.
To see how big it is, let's place a true-scale Earth beside it: 109 Earths line up side by side across its diameter, and 1. 3 million of them fit inside.
Its surface is 5,500 degrees, its core 15 million degrees; every second it converts 600 million tons of hydrogen into helium.
Now let's pull back and follow the journey of light: light leaving the Sun reaches Earth in 8 minutes and 20 seconds.
So every time you look at the Sun, you are actually seeing it as it was 8 minutes ago.
Uranus, the planet lying on its side: its axis is tilted 98 degrees.
So it practically rolls as it goes around the Sun; let's watch an 84-year trip from above.
Because of this, its poles spend 42 years in day and 42 years in night.
It looks blue-green because methane gas absorbs red light, and it too has thin, dark rings.
It is the first planet William Herschel discovered with a telescope, in 1781; only Voyager 2 saw it up close.
The James Webb Space Telescope, in 2023, imaged its rings and polar cap with this clarity.
Venus is considered Earth's twin in size; when we place them side by side, the difference is almost invisible.
But the resemblance ends there: the sulfuric acid clouds you see now completely hide the world beneath.
Let's remove the clouds: underneath lies a hell, heated to 465 degrees by the greenhouse effect of a thick carbon dioxide atmosphere, with a pressure 92 times Earth's.
Lead melts on the surface; the highest mountain here is Maxwell Montes, 11 kilometers high.
Only radar could see this surface; the Soviet Venera spacecraft lasted at most 2 hours after landing.
Venus also rotates backwards, and very slowly: one of its days is longer than one of its years.
